thread.title: Dividend payouts hit another record as tax bill-fueled giveaway to shareholders continues

author: Ryan Vlastelica
title: Dividend payouts hit another record as tax bill-fueled giveaway to shareholders continues
text:
Based on the giveaways from corporate America, there has never been a better time to be a stockholder.
According to S&P Dow Jones Indices, dividend payouts hit a record in the third quarter of 2018, the latest in a series of such records that has been matched by an even-more-aggressive avalanche of stock-buyback programs.
Rising dividends are common in the market, and according to Howard Silverblatt, senior index analyst at S&P Dow Jones Indices, “2018 is closing in on its seventh consecutive year of record dividend payments.”
See Also McConnell Is the Man in the Middle of the Kavanaugh Fight × The acceleration in growth stems in large part from the tax bill that was passed in late 2017, which gave corporations an influx of cash that they have in large part been using on shareholder-return programs.
Net dividend increases rose by $19.2 billion in the quarter, up from both the $15 billion increase in the year-ago period and the $13 billion net increase posted in the second quarter of this year, S&P Dow Jones Indices data showed. Aggregate increases — not including dividend decreases — were up $20.1 billion.
For the S&P 500 SPX, -0.94% , dividend payments set a record of $13.66 a share, up 11% year-over-year and jumping 4.3% from the second quarter, which had also been a record. In aggregate, companies in the S&P paid out $115.7 billion in the quarter, another record.
That data show there were 460 dividend increases reported during the third quarter, up 5% from the number of increases announced in the third quarter of 2017. Only 67 companies decreased their dividends, down 28% from the year-ago period. Currently, 81.4% of S&P 500 components pay a dividend; the index has an overall yield of 1.76%, according to FactSet.
Don’t miss: Stock-market dividend payouts are hitting records all over the world
In addition to increasing dividends, there has been a flurry of stock-buyback programs.
According to S&P Dow Jones Indices, companies in the S&P 500 spent a record $190.6 billion on stock buybacks in the second quarter of 2018. This represented growth of 58.7% from the second quarter of 2017. For the first half of the year, buybacks are up 49.9% to $379.7 billion. In August, Goldman Sachs estimated that $1 trillion could be spend on buyback programs in 2018.
“Though record amounts have been paid in dividends and buybacks, buybacks appear to be favored, as dividend payouts (dividends as a percentage of as-reported GAAP earnings) have declined, and are estimated to tick down,” Silverblatt wrote in a press release.
While the amount spent on buybacks is at records, the activity has been concentrated within a few stocks. Just 10 companies account for 78% of all buyback activity, according to Goldman, while Apple Inc. AAPL, -1.53% alone accounts for 24%.
